title: Good Feelings, Missouri and the Monroe Doctrine
short: Under Monroe one party dominated; Henry Clay's "American System" proposed a bank, tariffs and roads and canals; the Missouri Compromise (1820) balanced slave and free states and drew the 36°30' line; the Monroe Doctrine (1823) warned Europe against new colonies in the Americas.
trouble: Students think the Missouri Compromise settled slavery in the West for good. It postponed the conflict; it was repealed by the Kansas-Nebraska Act in 1854.

blocks.html: After the War of 1812 the Federalist Party faded, and James Monroe (1817 to 1825) governed with little organized opposition. A Boston newspaper called it an "era of good feelings" in 1817. Under the calm, three big issues took shape: the economy, slavery in the West, and the country's place in the world.

Henry Clay's American System proposed a national bank, a protective tariff, and roads and canals to tie the regions together. The Missouri Compromise (1820) admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state, and banned slavery in the rest of the Louisiana Purchase north of 36°30′. The Monroe Doctrine (1823) warned Europe against new colonies in the Americas.

Why did Missouri cause a crisis? In 1819 there were eleven free states and eleven slave states, so the Senate was evenly split. Missouri would tip the balance. A New York congressman, James Tallmadge, proposed gradually ending slavery there, and the House and Senate deadlocked along sectional lines. Thomas Jefferson wrote that the news woke him "like a fire bell in the night." Adding Maine kept the Senate even, and the line decided where slavery could spread in the rest of the territory.

doc.title: The Monroe Doctrine
doc.source: James Monroe, annual message to Congress, December 2, 1823
paras: The American continents, by the free and independent condition which they have assumed and maintain, are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers.

marks.note: Most of Spain's American colonies had just won independence.
Existing colonies were left alone; new ones were not to be made.

blocks.title: Reading the compromise
blocks.q: Could a settler hold enslaved people in the Arkansas Territory in 1825? In the land that later became Kansas?
steps: The Missouri Compromise drew the line at 36°30′ north across the rest of the Louisiana Purchase.
Arkansas lay south of the line, so slavery was allowed there.
Kansas lay north of the line (and was not Missouri), so slavery was banned there.
That ban held until the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 repealed it.
blocks.a: Arkansas: yes (south of the line). Kansas: no (north of the line), until 1854.

blocks.html: The Missouri Compromise did not settle slavery in the West for good. It postponed the fight for about thirty years. The Kansas-Nebraska Act repealed its line in 1854, and in 1857 the Supreme Court said Congress never had the power to draw it. Check: any question about the 1850s that treats the line as still in force is out of date.
